overview:
Four centuries of rule began in the wreckage of the Qin collapse, when Liu Bang, a village official turned warlord, outlasted his rival Xiang Yu and took the imperial title in 202 BCE. What he inherited was Qin's machinery — a centralized bureaucracy, standardized script and measures, a conscript army — attached to a lighter touch: lower taxes, fewer forced labor levies, and, for the first decades, a patchwork of semi-autonomous kingdoms held by kin and allies that later emperors gradually clawed back. From the capital at Chang'an, one of the two or three largest cities on earth at the time, the state grew into something without precedent in East Asia. Under Emperor Wu (141–87 BCE) it pushed hard in every direction: campaigns broke the power of the Xiongnu confederation on the steppe, commanderies were planted in the far south around Guangzhou and in northern Korea, and the envoy Zhang Qian's journeys into Central Asia opened the corridor of oasis routes later called the Silk Road, along which Chinese silk eventually reached Roman markets. Wu also made state patronage of Confucian learning official policy, founding an imperial academy and recruiting officials by recommendation and examination — the seed of a civil service that outlived every dynasty that used it.

The empire broke once in the middle. Wang Mang, a regent from a powerful consort family, took the throne in 9 CE and declared a new dynasty, the Xin, pairing his usurpation with sweeping reforms — land redistribution, restrictions on slavery, currency reissues — that alienated landowners and merchants alike. Catastrophic Yellow River flooding and famine turned dispossessed peasants into rebel armies, and by 23 CE he was dead and Chang'an sacked. A distant Liu-family claimant restored the dynasty in 25 CE and moved the capital east to Luoyang, and it is this Eastern Han that produced much of what people picture as Han civilization: paper as a practical writing material, Cai Lun's improvements to its manufacture around 105 CE, Zhang Heng's seismoscope and water-driven armillary sphere, Ban Chao's reassertion of Han authority across the Tarim Basin, and the first sustained Chinese contact with Buddhism arriving over the same routes. The state also counted itself with remarkable thoroughness: the census of 2 CE registered roughly 57.7 million people, the earliest surviving nationwide population figure from anywhere.

The ending was slow and internal. Court politics after about 90 CE settled into a grinding contest among child emperors, their mothers' families, and palace eunuchs, while land concentrated in the hands of great estate-holding clans whose tenants fell off the tax registers. When the Yellow Turban rising of 184 CE — a millenarian Daoist movement as much as a peasant revolt — spread across the north, the generals sent to crush it became the real powers, and the emperor a possession to be fought over. Cao Cao held the last Han ruler as a figurehead; his son Cao Pi accepted the throne's surrender in 220 CE, opening the Three Kingdoms period. The name stuck anyway: the ethnic majority of China still calls itself the Han.
significance: Han rule fixed the template that Chinese states would return to for the next two thousand years — a centralized bureaucratic empire staffed by men schooled in a canon, legitimated by the Mandate of Heaven, and defined against a steppe frontier it alternately fought, bribed, and traded with. Its dynastic histories, beginning with Sima Qian's Shiji and Ban Gu's Hanshu, created the form in which later Chinese history was written and thereby shaped what could be remembered. Outwardly, the Han opening of Central Asian routes stitched the eastern and western ends of Eurasia into a single, if indirect, commercial and epidemiological system that connected it to Kushan India, Parthian Iran, and Rome. And its name became an identity: "Han people," "Han characters," "Han language" all descend from a dynasty that ended eighteen centuries ago.
coverage: This dataset holds no events under the story, so nothing here can be shown on the map; the overview is written from general reference works rather than from mapped material, and the span given (205 BCE) is a placeholder near the conventional dates of 206 or 202 BCE. More broadly, nearly everything known about the Han comes through court-produced histories written by and for the literate official class, which means the record is thin on peasants, women outside consort families, and the non-Han peoples of the frontiers, and actively hostile toward losers — Wang Mang above all, whose reforms survive mostly in the accounts of those who overthrew him. Archaeology (tombs, bamboo-slip administrative documents from garrison sites) has begun to correct this, but unevenly.
